prices[i] is a stock's price on day i. Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell to maximize profit. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profitable trade exists.

data.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
data.summary: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the i-th day. You want to maximize your profit by choosing a single day to buy one stock and choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock. Return the maximum profit you can achieve from this transaction, or 0 if you cannot achieve any profit.

data.pattern_summary: Track the running minimum value seen so far while iterating through the array, using it to compute the optimal result at each step in linear time.

pattern_options.name: One-pass minimum tracking
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. Keeping track of the lowest price seen so far allows us to calculate the best potential profit at every single step without nested loops.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. While there are two variables of interest (buy and sell days), we only need a single forward pass through the array, not converging or diverging pointers.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Hash maps are used for finding complements or keeping frequency counts, but order matters here and we are looking for a global extrema relationship.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic programming
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Although this problem has an optimal substructure, it does not require a full memoization table because we only need the minimum price from the left.

signals.phrase: Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell
signals.hint: Implies a chronological order where the buy day must precede the sell day.
Signals that we need to find an optimal value over all valid pairs rather than just any valid pair.

data.brute_force_idea: Check every possible pair of buy and sell days where the sell day is after the buy day, calculate the profit for each pair, and keep track of the highest profit found.
data.brute_force_why: The outer loop runs n times and the inner loop runs roughly n times for each outer iteration, resulting in n * (n - 1) / 2 total comparisons.
data.bottleneck: The inner loop repeatedly compares every future day against the current buy day, recalculating differences from scratch even when we already checked those prices.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times each price is accessed inside the nested loops.
Ask yourself if you really need to pair every single day with every future day.
Think about what information from past days you could store in a variable instead of using a second loop.

data.overview: The algorithm tracks the minimum stock price seen so far and calculates the potential profit at each step, updating the maximum profit found. It works in a single pass because the best profit must come from selling at the current price after buying at the lowest historical price.
data.intuition: Imagine walking through a bazaar holding a basket. You always remember the cheapest price you've ever seen the item sold for. Every time you see a new price, you check how much profit you'd make if you sold it right now, and update your record if it's the best deal yet.

pitfalls: Failing to initialize min_price to infinity, causing it not to update on the first element.
Using nested loops which leads to an inefficient O(n^2) time complexity.
Returning the wrong value or negative numbers when prices strictly decrease.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach repeatedly checks every future day for every possible buy day, causing redundant work. The optimized solution removes this bottleneck by keeping a running track of the lowest price seen so far while doing a single pass over the array, letting us calculate the maximum profit instantly at each step.

derivation.note: Initializes the minimum price variable once.
Initializes the maximum profit variable once.
The loop iterates once for each element in the prices array.
Performs a constant time comparison against the current minimum price.
Performs a constant time profit check when the current price is not a new minimum.

data.time_summary: Lines 3 and 4 run once for O(1) time. The loop on line 5 runs n times, executing constant time operations inside it on lines 6 through 9. Summing these up gives O(n) total time, which is confirmed by the measured evidence showing step counts scaling linearly with n.
data.space_summary: We only store a few scalar variables (min_price and max_profit) regardless of the input size, which requires O(1) extra memory.
data.takeaway: When an array problem asks for an optimal value across pairs and a naive solution requires nested loops, look for a way to maintain state dynamically in a single pass.
mistakes: Using float('inf') without handling empty arrays, though constraints guarantee at least one element.
Forgetting to update the minimum price when a lower price is found, which breaks future profit calculations.
Confusing the index with the value when iterating directly over the array elements.
